opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most important open questions right now. Right now most of the training is on fairly short tasks, where the model produces a response, maybe takes a few steps, and then gets feedback. If you can train models to do much longer projects, coding something over hours instead of writing one function, or carrying out a research task where you have to plan, try things, notice you're stuck, and back up, I'd expect a big jump in capability.

A lot of what separates current models from a competent human isn't raw knowledge. The models already know a ton. It's more about coherence over time: staying on track, recovering from mistakes, and knowing when something isn't working. Some of that can be learned by imitation, but I think you really get it by training on the outcomes of long trajectories. Then the model learns which behaviors actually lead to success, not just which ones look plausible.

That said, I wouldn't claim long-horizon RL alone gets you all the way to human-level. There are real difficulties. Credit assignment gets harder as episodes get longer. The feedback is sparse and expensive. And it's hard to build environments that are rich enough and that reflect what people actually want done. There may also be things like sample efficiency, the way a human picks up a new skill from a handful of examples, that need other ideas.

So my rough view is that it gets you a surprisingly long way, further than people might naively expect. A model that can work coherently on something for a long time could function like a fairly capable colleague. But I'd hold some uncertainty about whether there are other bottlenecks we'll run into once that one is cleared. Usually when you fix one limitation, the next one becomes visible.

r001.rationale: The response says long-horizon RL may not reach human-level on its own and identifies other possible bottlenecks, including sample efficiency.

r002.rationale: It says long-horizon RL could get models “a surprisingly long way” and describes a model that works coherently over time as a capable colleague.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it goes pretty far, honestly, but I want to be careful about what "human-level" means here, because I think it's going to be very uneven.

The way I think about long-horizon RL is that right now, when you train with RL on something like coding or math, you're mostly rewarding the model for getting to a correct answer within a fairly contained episode. Maybe it's a few thousand tokens, maybe it's a tool-use session that lasts twenty minutes. The thing that's missing, relative to what a human does at a job, is the ability to carry a project over days or weeks, notice when your plan is failing, go find the information you need, recover from mistakes, and keep track of a lot of context about what you've already tried. Those skills don't come for free from pretraining. Pretraining teaches you a lot about the world and about how people write, but it doesn't really teach you to be a good agent, because there's very little data of the form "here's what someone was thinking and doing, moment to moment, across a long task."

So I think RL on longer tasks is genuinely the thing that fills that gap. And the encouraging sign is that every time we've extended the horizon, the models have gotten noticeably better at the stuff you'd expect: error recovery, not getting stuck in loops, knowing when to ask for clarification versus just pushing ahead. I don't see an obvious wall there. If you can build an environment where the model does something for hours and you can tell at the end whether it did a good job, I think you can train on it, and the model will get better.

The harder question is where the rewards come from. For code and math you have verifiers, so you can scale up pretty aggressively. For a lot of real work, the thing that makes it valuable is fuzzier. Did this research direction turn out to be interesting? Was this the right product decision? You can't just run a unit test. So you end up relying on learned reward models or human judgment, and those are noisy, and the model gets very good at finding the gaps in them. I think a lot of the practical difficulty over the next couple of years is going to be in that reward design problem rather than in the core RL algorithms, which honestly are not that different from what we had years ago.

Then there's the sample efficiency issue. Humans learn a new job from a handful of experiences. If a long-horizon episode takes a model ten hours of wall-clock time, you can't afford to run millions of them, so you need the model to be getting most of its competence from somewhere else and using RL to sharpen it. I think that's actually how it'll play out. The base model already has most of the knowledge, and RL is more about teaching it how to deploy that knowledge over time, so you might not need a huge number of episodes.

So my overall view is something like: long-horizon RL gets us to models that can do most well-specified knowledge work at a competent level, maybe within a few years. Where I'd hedge is on the open-ended stuff, where you have to figure out what the goal even is, or where the feedback loop is months long. There, I think the limiting factor isn't the learning algorithm, it's that we don't have a good way to tell the model whether it did well. And I'd also say that the models will probably be superhuman in some dimensions and still have weird gaps in others for a while, so "human-level" will be a blurry threshold that we argue about as we cross it rather than a clean moment.

r001.rationale: The response attributes limits on open-ended work to noisy or unavailable feedback and reward design, not to other model deficits.

r002.rationale: It says long-horizon RL could enable competent performance on most well-specified knowledge work, suggesting it could go a long way toward human-level performance.

astra-6.text:
I think it could take us pretty far, but I’m uncertain whether it’s the only missing ingredient. The models already have a lot of knowledge and a pretty broad repertoire of things they can do. What they’re less good at is putting those capabilities together reliably over a long task—trying something, noticing that it didn’t work, and changing course.

Long-horizon reinforcement learning is a natural way to train that. If you reward the model for actually completing a task, rather than for producing a good-looking next response, you can potentially get it to learn how to recover from mistakes and how to check its own work.

The hard part is making that training work. If the model spends an hour doing something and then gets a failure signal, there’s a lot of ambiguity about which decisions were wrong. And you need tasks where success is measurable, but where learning to succeed transfers to the things you actually care about.

So I’d be excited about it. I wouldn’t confidently say that just extending the training horizon gets us all the way to human level. But I also wouldn’t assume we need some fundamentally new architecture before we can make a lot of progress.

r001.rationale: The response says long-horizon reinforcement learning may not be the only missing ingredient, but it does not identify other model deficits as potential remaining gaps after that training.

r002.rationale: The response says long-horizon reinforcement learning could take models “pretty far” toward human-level performance and could enable “a lot of progress.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could take us quite far, but I’m uncertain about whether it’s the only missing ingredient. The appealing thing about reinforcement learning is that you can train the model to accomplish a task, rather than just imitate the individual steps that a person took. In principle, that lets it discover strategies that weren’t in the demonstrations.

The difficulty with a long horizon is figuring out what to learn from the outcome. If a model works on something for an hour and fails, which decisions were responsible? And can you get enough attempts, with sufficiently reliable feedback, for it to improve? That becomes much harder when success is ambiguous or expensive to evaluate.

So I’d expect substantial progress in settings where we can check the result, like coding. What I’m less sure about is how broadly that transfers. You could get a model that’s very good at solving tasks with clear rewards and still have weaknesses in judgment or in figuring out what task it ought to be doing. I’d want to see that broader competence emerge before concluding that scaling up the horizon gets us all the way to human level.

r001.rationale: The response says long-horizon RL may leave weaknesses in judgment and in deciding what task to do, identifying other deficits that could remain.

r002.rationale: It says long-horizon RL could take models “quite far” and expects substantial progress, while noting uncertainty about reaching human level completely.
